items.title: Reels vs. YouTube Shorts
items.description: A side-by-side visual comparison of short-form discovery, social reach, monetization and technical format. Red YouTube and magenta-purple Instagram cues give each platform its own visual lane.
items.prompt: Create a detailed landscape educational infographic titled “Reels vs. YouTube Shorts: The 2026 Short-Form Showdown”. Design for a university media-literacy presentation. Use a crisp white canvas, an oversized condensed black headline, a black-to-magenta-to-purple top banner, red YouTube Shorts symbols and Instagram gradient accents. Divide the layout into “The Specs & Discovery” on the left and “Monetization & Impact” on the right. Contrast search-led discovery and interest-based recommendations with social distribution and existing community. Use simple outlined icons for search, a brain, people, coins, a shopping bag, phones and links. Include discovery-duration indicators, a reach diagram, a compact technical-specification table, and a monetization comparison. Finish with a prominent decision panel explaining when each platform suits a creator's goal. Keep headings readable and tables aligned. Treat any supplied statistics, eligibility rules and revenue figures as dated claims that require source citations; do not invent benchmarks. The finished composition should feel like a structured editorial explainer, balancing scannable text with friendly illustrative diagrams.

Platform colors connect icons, tables and summary labels.
Large type makes the recommendation visible before the fine print.
A visible Gemini Notebook watermark remains in the supplied export.

items.title: Viral vs. Trending
items.description: A dark, colorful explainer separating long-tail sharing from short-lived cultural attention, with schematic curves and a three-card visual quiz.
items.prompt: Design a landscape university infographic titled “Viral vs. Trending: Aren’t They the Same Thing?” Use a deep midnight-navy background, large white sans-serif typography, cool cyan/lilac/green accents for VIRAL, and warm yellow/orange/coral accents for TRENDING. Place a globe with an explosive star on the left and a flaming clock on the right. Explain the difference through reach, lifespan, emotional triggers and distribution. Use one compact central comparison table with clear row alignment. Under the viral side draw a schematic S-curve with a tipping point and a long tail of engagement. Under the trending side draw a fast spike followed by decline. Label these diagrams as illustrative, not measured data. Add a small search-to-share illustration. Close with three rounded quiz cards showing an enduring cat meme, a recent dance challenge and a seasonal drink video; include short reasoned answers. Use bold display headings, rounded color blocks and playful geometric edge decoration. Avoid claiming fixed thresholds that universally define virality; cite any benchmark supplied in the source brief.

Curves translate time and attention into visual form.
A mini quiz moves the reader from definition to application.
Playful icons soften a text-heavy subject.

items.title: Your Phone Knows More
items.description: A central smartphone becomes a visual bridge between directly collected information and inferred behavioral profiles, ending in a privacy-audit checklist.
items.prompt: Create a landscape data-literacy infographic titled “YOUR PHONE KNOWS MORE ABOUT YOU THAN YOU THINK”. Place a large dark-screen smartphone vertically in the center on a light icy-blue background. Feed solid cyan and blue lines into its left edge from icons for GPS, microphone permissions, photo metadata, diagnostic logs, app activity and device sensors. Label this zone “Directly Collected Data”. From the right edge, extend dotted and curved blue-violet network paths into an anonymous profile silhouette and cloud, search and behavioral icons. Finish with a wide rounded “Quick 10-Minute Privacy Audit” panel covering location access, advertising controls and app-permission review. Use clear navy headings and a cyan-to-lilac accent gradient. Do not imply that every phone continuously records microphone audio; describe collection as conditional on apps, permissions and settings. Cite any percentage used.

items.title: Fake News: Can You Spot It?
items.description: A visual fact-checking challenge uses three implausible example posts and a verification checklist to teach skeptical reading.
items.prompt: Design a landscape media-literacy infographic titled “Fake News: Can You Spot It?” on a clean white background with pale blue panels, subtle teal geometric edges and a pink-to-orange title. The top third is a rounded blue “Real or Fake? Visual Challenge” tray containing three example-post cards: a glowing bottle claiming a miracle cure, an official-looking announcement claiming all weekend traffic is canceled, and a clearly fabricated shark swimming down a city street. Mark them as illustrative examples and use red-flag icons with a one-line explanation of the warning sign. Below, present credibility checks through illustrated white cards: investigate the source and date, read beyond the headline, seek evidence and independent corroboration, inspect images and emotional framing. Beside them show a large, simple verification workflow with stop, browser-search and trace-to-original icons. If it is labeled SIFT, represent all four original moves accurately: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to original context. Keep copy short, hierarchy consistent and source attribution visible. The goal is to teach a repeatable habit, not imply implausibility alone proves a claim false.

Red flags offer immediate visual feedback.
Rounded white cards and large icons support scanning.
Warm, yellow and teal workflow panels create a strong lower-page rhythm.

workflow: Create fictional practice examples without presenting them as real reports.
Write a source-evaluation checklist and verify the SIFT formulation.

items.title: A Moment Before Discovery
items.description: A quiet orchard scene: a seated young adult looks upward as a red apple appears suspended between the canopy and their face.
items.prompt: Create a photorealistic vertical editorial image of a young adult with tousled dark hair sitting on the grass at the base of a mature apple tree. Dress the subject in a charcoal relaxed long-sleeve top, loose faded blue-gray jeans and worn light-colored sneakers. Set the scene in a sunlit rural orchard with long grass, low hazy mountains, a pale sky, layered green leaves and a few red apples overhead. Frame the full seated figure from ground-level at a gentle three-quarter angle, leaving generous space around the canopy and landscape. Use natural late-afternoon light, soft rim highlights, detailed bark, believable skin and fabric, subtle film grain, muted olive and amber color grading, and realistic depth of field. The mood is quiet observation, an apple-and-gravity visual metaphor rather than a literal historical portrait. No text, logos or dramatic fantasy lighting. Preserve consistent identity, clothes, tree geometry and environmental lighting if generating a companion image. Keep the apple separated from the face with a readable silhouette and believable scale. Capture a suspended instant with restrained motion, maintaining the peaceful pastoral setting.

The downward apple and upward gaze create a clear visual relationship.

items.articleText:
Nepal Floods: A Disaster That Came Without Warning

Kathmandu, September 2, 2026: Nepal has been hit by severe floods that have caused heavy loss of life and property. The sudden floods damaged homes, roads, bridges and other important infrastructure. Rescue teams are working to find missing people and help those who have been affected.

The floods became especially dangerous after a sudden collapse of ice, rocks and a glacier in the Himalayan region sent a huge amount of water and debris into the river. The fast-moving water carried mud, rocks and other material downstream, giving people very little time to escape.

How did it happen?

The disaster started in the high Himalayan region. A large amount of ice and rock suddenly fell into a river system, causing the water level to rise quickly. The steep mountains made the water move at a very high speed towards the lower areas.

This turned the event into a flash flood, which is much more sudden and difficult to predict than a normal flood.

Why was the damage so serious?

Nepal has many steep mountains and narrow valleys. When a large amount of water enters these valleys suddenly, it can move very quickly and destroy everything in its path.

The floods damaged roads and bridges and affected electricity and hydropower projects. In some areas, rescue teams have also faced difficulties because roads were damaged and some communities became difficult to reach.

Is climate change connected?

Scientists have warned that the Himalayan region is becoming warmer. Rising temperatures can affect glaciers and make some mountain areas less stable. This can increase the risk of landslides, floods and other sudden disasters.

The Nepal floods have therefore raised concerns about the growing risks faced by communities living near the Himalayas.

The road to recovery

Even after the water started going down, the danger did not completely end. Rescue workers continued searching damaged areas and helping people who were trapped or had lost their homes. Authorities are also working to repair roads, restore electricity and provide basic support to affected families.

The Nepal floods show how quickly a natural event in the mountains can become a major disaster for people living far downstream. They also highlight the need for better warning systems, disaster preparation and climate awareness.
